stimulus.text:
The British print shows four Loyalists hanged from a tree branch, with the words “Recommended to Congress by Lord S—” written above them. Below, three Native figures attack Loyalists: one holds a rope and says “I have them all in a String,” one holds a knife and says “I'll scalp him,” and one raises a tomahawk and says “I'll tomahawk the Dog.” A kneeling Loyalist cries, “O Cruel Fate! is this the Return for Our Loyalty.” The title reads “The Savages let loose, OR The Cruel FATE of the LOYALISTS,” with the captions “Is this a Peace, when Loyalists must bleed?” and “It is a Bloody Piece of work indeed.”
— The Savages Let Loose, London, 1783 (sold by W. Humphrey, 227 Strand)

stem: A historian would best use the print's depiction of Native people as evidence of

options.text: British attitudes toward Native peoples, not what Native peoples did
A factual record of Native attacks on Loyalists in 1783
options.misconception: The print is a London cartoon imagining a feared fate, not a witness's record; it shows no real event.

options.text: Native peoples' own account of their role in the war
options.misconception: Native peoples drew no part of this print; a London artist drew them as his British audience expected to see them.

options.text: The Continental Congress's official policy toward Native peoples
options.misconception: Congress made no policy in this print; it is a British satire, not an American government document.

rationales.A: The printmaker draws Native people as wild attackers with tomahawks and scalping knives because that is how his London audience imagined them. The image proves British prejudice, not Native conduct.
rationales.B: No attack like this is recorded; the print warns of a fate its maker fears, and it was drawn in London, far from the scene.
rationales.C: The print gives Native peoples no voice of their own; every word in it is the London artist's, not theirs.
rationales.D: Congress appears only in the line “Recommended to Congress by Lord S—”; the print is British satire, not American policy.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who drew it. A London printmaker in 1783, for a British audience.
2. Ask what he shows. Native figures as savage attackers — a caricature, not a portrait.
3. Ask what it proves. What Britons feared and believed about Native peoples, not what Native peoples did.
Remember: an image proves its maker's mind before it proves its subject — ask who holds the pen.
